slides.title: Testing where failure would hurt most
points: There's never time to test everything equally. A risk-based strategy spends effort where the likelihood and impact of failure are highest.
It turns 'test everything' into a plan people can agree on.

slides.title: Likelihood × impact
points: List features and changes; rate how likely each is to break (new, complex, changed often) and how bad that would be (money, safety, data, reputation).
High-risk areas get deep testing at several layers; low-risk ones get a light check.
Revisit the ratings as the product and incidents change.
Share the plan with product and engineering, including what won't be tested.

slides.title: Explicit gaps
points: Writing down what isn't tested feels uncomfortable and is honest.
Ratings are judgement calls; use incident history and data where you can.
Low-risk areas still break sometimes; monitoring in production backs up testing.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A risk matrix in the release plan.
Payments, sign-in and data deletion always in the high-risk group.
Exploratory sessions aimed at the riskiest changes.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Learning, designing and testing at once
points: Exploratory testing is skilled, unscripted investigation: the tester uses what each step reveals to choose the next.
It finds bugs scripted tests weren't written to look for.

slides.title: Charters and time boxes
points: A charter gives a focus: 'Explore checkout with unusual addresses to find data-handling problems.'
A time box (60–90 minutes) keeps sessions focused.
Notes record what was tried, what was found and questions raised.
Heuristics guide ideas: boundaries, interruptions, odd data, different devices, going back and forth.

slides.title: Depth against repeatability
points: Exploration finds surprising bugs but isn't repeatable like automation.
It depends on the tester's skill and knowledge of the product.
Its findings should become automated checks where useful.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Session-based test management with debriefs.
Bug bashes before big releases.
Exploration paired with developers on new features.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: 'How would you test this?'
points: Interviewers name something (a login page, a lift, a search box) and ask how you'd test it.
They're scoring structure, coverage and prioritisation.

slides.title: A structure to follow
points: Clarify requirements and users first.
Cover functional cases, edge and negative cases, then non-functional ones: performance, security, accessibility, usability.
Use named techniques (boundaries, partitions, state transitions).
Prioritise: what you'd test first and what you'd automate.

slides.title: Breadth with judgement
points: Listing 50 cases without priority shows less than 10 well-chosen ones.
Ask questions; assumptions change the answer.
Mention how you'd know it works in production.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Practise on everyday objects and simple web features.
Know a few techniques by name and example.
End with risks and what you'd automate.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Write a working test, live
points: SDET interviews often ask you to automate a scenario: a UI flow with Playwright or Selenium, or an API test.
They're checking clean code, stable selectors, waits and assertions.

slides.title: What good looks like
points: Clear arrange-act-assert structure.
Robust locators and condition-based waits.
Meaningful assertions on outcomes, not on implementation details.
Independent tests with their own data, and readable names.

slides.title: Done and right
points: A working simple test beats an unfinished framework.
Explain what you'd add with more time (page objects, data setup, CI).
Avoid sleeps; say why.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Write a few tests against a public demo app.
Practise API tests with assertions on status and body.
Talk while coding.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Regular time for each person
points: A one-to-one is a recurring private conversation between a manager and each report, usually weekly or every two weeks.
It's the report's meeting more than the manager's.

slides.title: Their agenda, consistently
points: Let them bring topics first: blockers, concerns, ideas, career.
Keep it regular; cancelling often tells people they don't matter.
Ask open questions, listen more than you talk, and follow up on what you promised.
Use some sessions for longer-term topics: growth, goals, feedback both ways.

slides.title: Not a status meeting
points: Turning one-to-ones into project updates wastes the one private channel.
Too rigid an agenda stifles; no structure drifts.
Some people need prompting to raise concerns; ask directly.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A shared running doc of topics and actions.
Thirty minutes, protected on the calendar.
Early warning of problems because people trust the space.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Helping people see what works and what doesn't
points: Feedback is specific information about someone's behaviour and its effect, given so they can keep doing it or change.
Frequent small feedback beats a big annual surprise.

slides.title: Situation, behaviour, impact
points: Describe the situation, the specific behaviour, and its impact ('In Tuesday's review, you interrupted Sam twice; Sam stopped sharing ideas').
Give positive feedback as specifically as corrective feedback.
Give it soon, in private for corrections, and ask for their view.
Ask for feedback on yourself, and act on it.

slides.title: Kind and clear
points: Softening too much hides the message; harshness shuts people down.
Feedback about personality ('you're careless') can't be acted on; behaviour can.
Saving feedback for reviews makes it stale and surprising.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Feedback in one-to-ones as a habit, not an event.
Peer feedback gathered before reviews.
Follow-up to see whether things changed.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Giving work away well
points: Delegation hands ownership of work to someone else, with the context and authority to do it.
Managers who don't delegate become the bottleneck and stop their team growing.

slides.title: Outcome, context, authority
points: Describe the outcome and why it matters, not every step.
Share constraints and the decisions they can make alone.
Agree check-in points matched to their experience.
Match the task to their growth: stretch, with support.

slides.title: Short-term speed against long-term capacity
points: Doing it yourself is faster this week and slower forever.
Delegating without context sets people up to fail.
Taking work back at the first problem teaches people not to try.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Clear owners for projects and decisions.
Regular check-ins rather than surprise reviews at the end.
Credit given publicly to the person who did the work.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

newQuestions.stem: A release changes the payment flow and the 'About us' page. You have one day. How do you split testing?
choices: Most effort on the payment flow (high impact, complex change), a quick check of the About page
Only the About page, it's quicker
why: Effort follows risk: money paths first.

newQuestions.stem: Which is a good exploratory testing charter?
choices: 'Explore the file upload with large, empty and oddly named files to find failures in validation and error messages' (90 minutes)
why: Focused area, technique and goal, time-boxed.

newQuestions.stem: Asked 'How would you test a login page?', what's the strongest opening?
choices: Ask about requirements (password rules, lockout, SSO, 2FA, who uses it), then cover functional, negative, security and accessibility cases by priority
why: Clarifying and structuring show test thinking.

newQuestions.stem: In a live automation exercise you add `sleep(5000)` before clicking a button. What will the interviewer likely say?
choices: Use a wait for the button to be visible and enabled instead; fixed sleeps are slow and still flaky
why: Condition-based waits are faster and reliable.
Then it fails on slow loads.

newQuestions.stem: A new manager uses one-to-ones to go through each report's ticket status. What's being lost?
choices: The private space for the report's concerns, growth and feedback; status belongs in the team's tools or stand-ups
why: One-to-ones are where trust and early warnings come from.

newQuestions.stem: Which is the most useful corrective feedback?
choices: 'In yesterday's incident call, you started changing production without telling the commander; two fixes clashed. Next time, announce changes first.'
why: Specific behaviour, impact, and what to do next.

newQuestions.stem: A manager delegates a project but then rewrites the person's design doc without discussion. What's the likely effect?
choices: The person loses ownership and motivation, and stops bringing their best thinking; discuss changes instead
why: Taking work back undermines delegation and trust.
